title: Exploratory Causal Inference in SAEnce
claim: Discovering unknown treatment effects from raw trial data can be done by chaining representation, sparse decomposition, statistical selection, and expert interpretation.
layout: 4 stages, left-to-right, numbered captions below, trapezoid encoder shapes
description: A horizontal four-stage flow with lowercase roman-numeral captions and small icons: i. experiment, ii. represent, iii. select, iv. interpret. At far left is a stack of petri-dish photos with ants, overlaid with a yellow patch grid. A dark-blue trapezoid labeled FM narrows into a rounded column of three gradient circles (embeddings). A coral trapezoid labeled SAE expands into a taller column of five gradient circles (sparse neurons). A large sage-green rectangle labeled NES follows. Two selected neuron circles then feed two pale trapezoids, each leading to a 2x4 grid of petri-dish photos that show contrasting ant behavior. The palette is muted blue, coral and green. The eye goes first to the large colored blocks, then right to the photos.
caption: Pipeline for Exploratory Causal Inference: (i) collect experimental data, (ii) extract interpretable representations via a Foundation Model and Sparse Autoencoder, (iii) identify treatment effects via Neural Effect Search, and (iv) interpret the causal findings, i.e., affected neurons, with domain experts.
abstract: Randomized Controlled Trials are one of the pillars of science; nevertheless, they rely on hand-crafted hypotheses and expensive analysis. Such constraints prevent causal effect estimation at scale, potentially anchoring on popular yet incomplete hypotheses. We propose to discover the unknown effects of a treatment directly from data. For this, we turn unstructured data from a trial into meaningful representations via pretrained foundation models and interpret them via a sparse autoencoder. However, discovering significant causal effects at the neural level is not trivial due to multiple-testing issues and effects entanglement. To address these challenges, we introduce Neural Effect Search, a novel recursive procedure solving both issues by progressive stratification. After assessing the robustness of our algorithm on semi-synthetic experiments, we showcase, in the context of experimental ecology, the first successful unsupervised causal effect identification on a real-world scientific trial.
